A pull request does not run them. Someone with write access to the repository can run them on a branch with gh workflow run tests.yml --ref <branch>.

Name test files *_test.py. A test that needs AWS or Kafka must be marked with @pytest.mark.integration, or be in one of the modules that tests/conftest.py marks as a whole. A live test that creates an IAM user, a namespace, a topic or a consumer group takes its names from live_subject() or live_namespace() in tests/live_identity, or from the random_subject fixture in tests/conftest.py, which calls live_subject(). The live tests' IAM identity can touch only resources with those names, and the nightly sweep, a script that deletes what live runs leave behind, finds only those (Naming live-test resources).

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
pyproject.toml lists the service's dependencies, and two files generated by uv lock their versions for Python 3.14 on Linux x86_64, the image's platform:

  • requirements.txt locks the service's dependencies. The image and CI install it.
  • requirements-dev.txt locks the dev tools, at the same versions for the packages the two files share. CI installs it, and the image does not.

After you change the dependencies in pyproject.toml, regenerate both files from the repository root, requirements.txt first, since it constrains the other:

uv pip compile pyproject.toml --python-version 3.14 --python-platform x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --exclude-newer 2026-10-26T12:00:00Z -o requirements.txt
uv pip compile pyproject.toml --extra dev -c requirements.txt --python-version 3.14 --python-platform x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu --exclude-newer 2026-10-26T12:00:00Z -o requirements-dev.txt

Each file's header holds the command that generated it. uv ignores releases published after the --exclude-newer time, so the commands give the same versions on any machine, and it keeps the versions already in a file where it can. To move every package to its newest release, add --upgrade to both commands and set --exclude-newer to the current date.

Dependabot proposes updates to both files once a month, in one pull request. It edits the pinned versions in place and keeps each header as it is, but it does not run uv: the --exclude-newer date stays, and a package that an updated one newly needs is not added. If the unit tests fail on such a pull request, regenerate the files with --upgrade instead. Dependabot also proposes new builds and patch releases of the image's Python 3.14, but not a new minor or major version of Python.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
Each change that users can see, such as a new route or a change to a response, gets a release:

  1. In the pull request that makes the change, bump version in pyproject.toml.

  2. Once it is merged, tag the commit on main with v and the version, and push the tag:

    git tag vX.Y.Z <commit>
git push origin vX.Y.Z

  3. Publish a GitHub release from the tag, with notes that GitHub generates from the pull requests merged since the previous release:

    gh release create vX.Y.Z --verify-tag --generate-notes

The service reports its version, followed by + and the first 12 characters of the commit its image was built from, as info.version in /openapi.json, and the API documentation at / shows it:

curl -sS https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/openapi.json | jq -r .info.version

docs.title: Commits and pull requests
docs.text:
• Branch from main, and name the branch after the kind of change and its subject, such as fix/consistent-reads, ci/split-unit-and-live-tests or docs/deploy-guide-and-runbook. The prefixes in use are feat/, fix/, ci/, docs/ and chore/.
  • Write the commit subject and the pull request title as an imperative sentence that says what changes, such as "Read DynamoDB items with strong consistency".
  • In the pull request description, say what changed and why, and whether merging deploys the service.
  • Pull requests are squash-merged: the title, followed by the pull request number, becomes the subject of the one commit on main.

docs.title: What merging does
docs.text:
A merge is a push to main, which starts these workflows:

  • deployment.yml runs the unit tests and then deploys the service to production, unless every changed file is under docs/, is a Markdown file, or is mkdocs.yml (What triggers a deploy). A deploy restarts the service, which drops every consumer instance.
  • tests.yml runs the unit tests and the live tests.
  • docs.yml builds the docs and publishes them to GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This startup script is designed for the Diaspora Admin Console running on the AWS Lightsail instance kafbat-ui at 34.201.83.114. It automates the setup of a Docker environment, installs Docker Compose, and configures a Kafbat UI (v1.5.0) service with essential security and environment settings. Additionally, it establishes a systemd service for managing the Docker Compose application, redirects HTTP traffic from port 80 to port 8080, and schedules an automated reboot every three days.

docs.title: Masked Credentials
docs.text:
The script includes sensitive credentials that have been masked for security purposes:

  • SPRING_SECURITY_USER_NAME: ******** (Web login username)
  • SPRING_SECURITY_USER_PASSWORD: ******** (Web login password)
  • AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: ******************** (Used for connecting to MSK)
  • AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY: **************************** (Used for connecting to MSK)

docs.title: AWS Lightsail Configuration
docs.text:
To deploy this instance, follow these steps:

  1. Create an Instance:
  2. Navigate to AWS Lightsail.
  3. Choose OS: Linux/Unix → OS only → Ubuntu 24.04 LTS.
  4. Paste the script below into Add launch script, so it initializes and configures the instance.
  5. Allocate at least 1 GB memory and 2 vCPUs for optimal performance.

  6. Set the instance name to kafbat-ui.

  7. Assign a Static IP:

  8. Go to Lightsail → Networking.
  9. Create a static IP in us-east-1, naming it kafbat-ui-static-ip, and attach it to kafbat-ui.

The running instance, created in September 2025, uses Lightsail's WordPress blueprint (Debian 12) instead of Ubuntu, so its login user is bitnami.

docs.title: Startup Script
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash

# adapted from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mikegcoleman/todo/master/lightsail-compose.sh
# and https://stackoverflow.com/a/33370375

# Set the front-end for apt to noninteractive to avoid prompts during package installation
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Update package list and perform a dist-upgrade with forced configuration file overwrite
# apt-get update && apt-get -o Dpkg::Options::="--force-confold" dist-upgrade -q -y --force-yes
apt-get update && apt-get -o Dpkg::Options::="--force-confold" dist-upgrade -q -y --allow-downgrades

# Install Docker
curl -sSL https://get.docker.com | sh

# Add the ubuntu user to the docker group
usermod -aG docker ubuntu

# Install Docker Compose
curl -L https://github.com/docker/compose/releases/download/v2.33.1/docker-compose-$(uname -s)-$(uname -m) -o /usr/local/bin/docker-compose
chmod +x /usr/local/bin/docker-compose

# Create a directory for Docker configuration
mkdir /srv/docker

# Create a Docker Compose configuration file
cat <<EOF > /srv/docker/docker-compose.yml
services:
  kafbat-ui:
    container_name: kafbat-ui
    image: ghcr.io/kafbat/kafka-ui:v1.5.0
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    environment:
      - DYNAMIC_CONFIG_ENABLED=true
      # Refresh cluster statistics every 5 minutes, not every 30 s (see Broker CPU credits below)
      - KAFKA_UPDATE_METRICS_RATE_MILLIS=300000
      - AUTH_TYPE=LOGIN_FORM
      - SPRING_SECURITY_USER_NAME=******
      - SPRING_SECURITY_USER_PASSWORD=******
      - AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=******
      - AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=******
    volumes:
      - /srv/docker/config.yml:/etc/kafkaui/dynamic_config.yaml
EOF

# Create a Kafka UI configuration file
cat <<EOF > /srv/docker/config.yml
kafka:
  clusters:
    - name: diaspora
      bootstrapServers: b-1-public.diaspora.jdqn8o.c18.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9198,b-2-public.diaspora.jdqn8o.c18.kafka.us-east-1.amazonaws.com:9198
      properties:
        security.protocol: SASL_SSL
        sasl.mechanism: AWS_MSK_IAM
        sasl.client.callback.handler.class: software.amazon.msk.auth.iam.IAMClientCallbackHandler
        sasl.jaas.config: software.amazon.msk.auth.iam.IAMLoginModule required awsProfileName="default";
EOF

# Download the systemd service file for Docker Compose application
curl -o /etc/systemd/system/docker-compose-app.service https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zahedahmed/todo/master/docker-compose-app.service

# Enable the Docker Compose application service
systemctl enable docker-compose-app

# Start the Docker Compose application in detached mode
docker-compose -f /srv/docker/docker-compose.yml up -d

# Redirect port 80 to port 8080 using iptables
iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j REDIRECT --to-port 8080

# Install iptables-persistent to save iptables rules
apt-get install -y iptables-persistent
netfilter-persistent save

# Schedule a reboot every 3 days at 4:30 AM
(crontab -l 2>/dev/null; echo "30 4 */3 * * /sbin/reboot") | crontab -

docs.title: Upgrading Kafbat UI
docs.text:
The instance runs the image tag pinned in /srv/docker/docker-compose.yml. Docker does not pull a newer image by itself, and the reboot every three days restarts the same image. To move to a new Kafbat UI release:

  1. Connect over SSH as bitnami, from the Lightsail console or with a temporary key from aws lightsail get-instance-access-details --instance-name kafbat-ui --protocol ssh.
  2. Back up the compose file, change the tag on its image: line, then pull and restart: 
    cd /srv/docker
sudo cp -p docker-compose.yml docker-compose.yml.bak
sudoedit docker-compose.yml
sudo docker-compose pull
sudo docker-compose up -d
  3. Check that sudo docker ps shows the new tag and that the login page loads. Kafbat UI takes about two minutes to start on this instance.

To roll back, restore docker-compose.yml.bak and run the last two commands again.

docs.title: Broker CPU credits
docs.text:
The diaspora cluster's brokers are kafka.t3.small instances, which run on CPU credits. Each broker earns 24 credits an hour and holds at most 576; a broker that runs out is throttled to its baseline.

Kafbat UI refreshes its cluster statistics on a timer. Each refresh reads every topic and its configuration, the earliest and latest offsets of every partition, every consumer group and its offsets, and each broker's log directories. In October 2026, with the default refresh of 30 s, the console's load spent broker 1's credits, and topic creation and deletion stalled until the instance was stopped. KAFKA_UPDATE_METRICS_RATE_MILLIS=300000 sets the refresh to 5 minutes, so the topic sizes and consumer lag the console shows can be up to 5 minutes old.

After any change to the console, watch each broker's CPUCreditBalance in CloudWatch (namespace AWS/Kafka, dimensions Cluster Name and Broker ID). If it keeps falling, stop the instance; its static IP keeps the address for the next start.

docs.title: API Reference
docs.text:
• Live docs
  • Live openapi.json

The web service has three REST APIs. Each has a reference page that gives every route with a curl example, its request, its replies and its limits.

API Routes Does Management /api/v3/user, /api/v3/key, /api/v3/namespace, /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic} Creates and deletes the user, its access key and its topics, and lists its namespaces and topics Produce /api/v3/{namespace}/topics/{topic}/records and records:batch Writes records to a topic, in the request syntax of Confluent's REST API v3 Consume /api/v2/consumers Reads records through consumer instances, in the paths and bodies of Confluent's REST Proxy v2

All three run over HTTPS on port 443 with a Globus token. A client starts with POST /api/v3/key, which creates the user and its default namespace, or POST /api/v3/user, which creates them without a key; then it creates a topic, produces to it and consumes from it. The access key that POST /api/v3/key returns lets a Kafka client connect to the cluster directly instead; the produce and consume routes need no key.

docs.title: Getting subject and authorization
docs.text:
Every endpoint requires a subject header (your Globus OpenID sub claim) and an authorization header (a Globus OAuth2 Bearer token). The diaspora-event-sdk gets both:

pip install diaspora-event-sdk

from diaspora_event_sdk import Client as GlobusClient

c = GlobusClient()  # triggers Globus login flow on first use

subject = c.subject_openid
authorizer = c.authorizer or c.app.get_authorizer(c.DIASPORA_RESOURCE_SERVER)
authorization = authorizer.get_authorization_header()
namespace = c.namespace

print(f'export SUBJECT="{subject}"')
print(f'export AUTHORIZATION="{authorization}"')
print(f'export NAMESPACE="{namespace}"')

Use these values in the subject and authorization headers when you call the routes of each API's page.

$NAMESPACE is the user's default namespace: ns- followed by the last 12 characters of the subject without dashes. The default namespace exists once POST /api/v3/user or POST /api/v3/key has run.

docs.title: Try it out
docs.text: Once you have your subject and authorization, you can interact with the live API directly from the Swagger UI. Click "Try it out" and fill in the header fields on each endpoint. Each API's page gives a curl example for every route.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
The management routes and the produce and consume routes report errors in two shapes.

The management routes answer HTTP 200, for a failure as for a success, with status in the body: "success" or "failure" with a message, or "error" with a reason when the token check fails (Replies):

{"status": "failure", "message": "Topic my-topic not found in ns-0123456789ab"}

The produce and consume routes answer an HTTP status that says what happened, and a failure's body is {"error_code": <int>, "message": <str>}, with Confluent's five-digit codes (produce errors, consume errors):

{"error_code": 40401, "message": "Topics not found in namespace ns-0123456789ab: my-topic"}

These replies differ from the two shapes:

  • A failed token check on a produce route answers 401 with the management routes' body, {"status": "error", "reason": ...}. On a consume route it answers 401 with {"error_code": 40101, "message": ...}.
  • A request without the subject or authorization header answers 422. A management or produce route gives FastAPI's {"detail": [...]}, which names each missing header; a consume route gives {"error_code": 422, "message": ...}.
  • A path that matches no route answers 404, and a method a route does not take 405, both with FastAPI's {"detail": <str>}.
  • An error the service does not handle answers 500: with {"error_code": 500, "message": "Internal server error"} on a consume route, and with the text Internal Server Error on the others.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
The Diaspora Event SDK calls these routes from Python; its README shows how. Its examples run against the live service:

  • DiasporaDemo.ipynb: logging in, the management routes through the SDK, and producing and consuming with a Kafka client and the access key.
  • ConsumerRESTDemo.ipynb: producing and consuming over the produce and consume routes, first with plain HTTP requests and then with the SDK.

docs.title: Consume API
docs.text:
The consumer routes take the paths and bodies of Confluent's REST Proxy v2, under /api/v2/consumers. They act in the caller's default namespace, ns- and the last 12 characters of the subject without dashes ($NAMESPACE). Topics are named without the namespace, and the group my-group is the Kafka consumer group $NAMESPACE.my-group. Every route takes the subject and authorization headers (Getting subject and authorization).

The SDK's RESTConsumer wraps these routes, and creates an instance again when the service has dropped it (Instance lifecycle). ConsumerRESTDemo.ipynb consumes records with plain HTTP requests and then with the SDK.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Create consumer instance
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v2/consumers/my-group" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.kafka.v2+json" \
  -d '{"name": "my-instance", "format": "json", "auto.offset.reset": "earliest"}'

{"instance_id": "my-instance", "base_uri": "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v2/consumers/my-group/instances/my-instance"}

export INSTANCE="https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v2/consumers/my-group/instances/my-instance"

# Subscribe to a list of topics (topic patterns are not supported)
curl -X POST "$INSTANCE/subscription" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/vnd.kafka.v2+json" \
  -d '{"topics": ["my-topic"]}'

# Fetch records of a json instance
curl -X GET "$INSTANCE/records?timeout=5000" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION" \
  -H "Accept: application/vnd.kafka.json.v2+json"

[{"topic": "my-topic", "key": null, "value": {"step": 7, "loss": 0.31}, "partition": 0, "offset": 12, "headers": [{"name": "trace", "value": "AAE="}]}]

# Commit offsets
curl -X POST "$INSTANCE/offsets" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

# Delete consumer instance
curl -X DELETE "$INSTANCE" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

docs.text:
In this table, … stands for /api/v2/consumers/{group}/instances/{instance}. A route with no body in the table takes none.

base_uri is the instance's absolute URL. The scheme and host come from the X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host headers when present and when they hold a plain scheme (http or https) and host, and otherwise from the request's Host and scheme.

A request body may have the content type application/vnd.kafka.v2+json, another v2 type (application/vnd.kafka.binary.v2+json, application/vnd.kafka.json.v2+json and the avro, jsonschema and protobuf ones), application/json, or none. Any other type is refused with 415 and error code 415. Every reply but a fetch's has the type application/vnd.kafka.v2+json.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
A fetch chooses its reply's type from the Accept header, as Confluent's REST Proxy does. application/vnd.kafka.binary.v2+json, application/vnd.kafka.v2+json, */* or no Accept reads a binary instance, and application/vnd.kafka.json.v2+json reads a json instance; the reply has the type chosen. A type of the other format is refused with 406 and error code 40601. An Accept that names no v2 type, such as application/json, is refused with 406 and error code 406. HTTP libraries that send Accept: */* or application/json by default must set the header to read a json instance.

Each record is {"topic", "key", "value", "partition", "offset", "headers"}, as in Confluent's REST Proxy v2, plus headers in the produce routes' form: a list of {"name": string, "value": base64 string or null}. A binary instance returns keys and values as base64, so it returns the bytes exactly. A json instance returns a key or value that is one JSON value as that value, written as it was produced, and any other UTF-8 text as a JSON string of the text. So the produce routes' JSON keys and values come back as JSON, and STRING ones as strings. A client cannot tell "abc" produced as JSON from abc produced as text; produce JSON-typed keys and values for json instances, or read with a binary instance.

A json instance cannot return a key or value that is not UTF-8. A record with one ends its partition's part of the reply: the records before it are returned, the partition is sought back to it, and the other partitions go on. A fetch whose first record has one is refused with 408 and error code 40801, and so is every fetch after it, until the client seeks past the record or reads it with a binary instance. The check that a key or value is one JSON value is stricter than Confluent's: text after the value, as in {"a":1} {"b":2}, makes the whole of it text. A check that would take more than 32 MiB of memory is not made, and the value is returned as text. A JSON string of ASCII text is checked up to about 15 MiB, larger than any record, but an array of small objects ([{"a":1},...]) only up to about 1.5 MiB, and a deeply nested array less.

docs.title: Instances, fetches and commits
docs.text:
A consumer instance serves one request at a time. A request that waits more than 10 seconds for another request on the same instance returns 409 with error code 40904; retry it. A fetch does not wait: if another request holds the instance, it returns 409 with 40904 at once.

At create, the group and name are each 1 to 128 letters, digits, dots, dashes or underscores, starting with a letter or a digit; without a name, the service picks 12 hex digits. Confluent's deprecated id field, if set, is taken as the name. auto.offset.reset must be earliest, latest (the default) or none, and auto.commit.enable must be true or false (the default), in any case. fetch.min.bytes and consumer.request.timeout.ms must be whole numbers of at least 0, given as numbers or strings. A create that breaks one of these rules is refused with 422 and error code 42204, and the message names the group, the name or the setting. fetch.min.bytes is passed to the Kafka consumer. consumer.request.timeout.ms is how long a fetch that names no timeout waits for records, 5000 ms if it is not set; it is not passed to the Kafka consumer.

A fetch waits for records for its timeout, in milliseconds. A timeout of 0 or less, or none, waits for the instance's consumer.request.timeout.ms. Either wait is capped at 30000 ms. As in Confluent's REST Proxy, max_bytes counts the bytes of the records' keys and values, and a reply holds fewer than that; unlike there, the first record is returned however large. 0, a negative value or none sets no limit but the reply's 2 MiB. The records left out come first in the next fetch. A fetch polls in turns of at most half a second (see Limits), and its turns and its waits for a turn together take no longer than its timeout. It returns as soon as a turn finds records, and returns [] if none did.

A commit with offsets names, for each partition, the offset of the last record the client processed, as in Confluent's REST Proxy, and the group commits the next one, with the offset's metadata if given. A commit without a body commits the position of each assigned partition, which is already the next record to read. So after a commit of offset 41, or after a commit without a body once a fetch returned offset 41, GET …/offsets returns 42 for that partition. It leaves out a partition the group has not committed, and a request without a body is refused with 404 and 40402, as in Confluent's REST Proxy.

An instance returns records as binary or json, named in format in any case. Octopus runs no schema registry, so a create with avro, jsonschema or protobuf is refused with 422, as is any other format.

Every topic has one partition, 0, and a request that names another partition is refused with 404. A seek or a commit with offsets takes only partitions assigned to the instance. A partition is assigned by assignments, or after a subscribe by the group once the instance has fetched. A seek or commit on any other partition is refused with 409. A seek to the beginning or end with an empty list seeks every assigned partition, and is refused with 409 if none is assigned. An instance either subscribes to topics or is assigned partitions: to switch, unsubscribe first, or the request is refused with 409.

A subscribe or an assign takes only topics the namespace holds, and refuses any other with 404 and 40401. A topic the namespace holds but the cluster does not list, such as one deleted while an instance reads it, is not created by the subscription or the assignment: the instance's fetches return no records from it.

docs.title: Instance lifecycle
docs.text:
An instance lives in the memory of the one worker that created it. A deploy or a restart of the service drops every instance, and an instance idle for CONSUMER_INSTANCE_TIMEOUT_MS (5 minutes by default; the service looks every 30 s) is closed. The next request for an instance that is gone gets 404 with error code 40403.

An instance created with auto.commit.enable set to true commits its positions at these times, and no others:

  • During a fetch, when 5 s or more have passed since its last commit: the Kafka consumer commits the positions it had before that fetch's poll.
  • When it is assigned partitions or unsubscribes, and, while it is subscribed, before its group rebalances during a fetch: the Kafka consumer commits its positions first.
  • When it is deleted, when the service closes it for being idle, and when the service shuts down, before it closes. The commit waits at most 5 s; at shutdown, all the instances share 8 s.

Its position in a partition is the record after the last one a fetch returned to the client: records that a reply left out, that did not reach the client, or that a fetch cancelled at shutdown had polled are sought back to before any commit. An idle instance stays in its consumer group until the service closes it, so the commit at that close goes through. A commit that fails or runs out of time is logged, and the instance closes anyway, so the group keeps its earlier commit; at shutdown, an instance still busy after 8 s is neither committed nor closed. An instance without auto-commit commits nothing by itself: only the client's commits count.

After a 404 with 40403, the client creates the instance again with the same group and name, subscribes or assigns again, and fetches. The group starts from its last commit, so the records fetched after that commit come again; a client that needs each record once should carry an id in the record and drop repeats. A group that has never committed starts where the instance's auto.offset.reset says, and with latest, the default, it skips the records produced while no instance was reading.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
The consumer routes have these limits:

  • A user (subject) may hold 4 consumer instances, and the service 12 in all. A create past either is refused with 429.
  • A request may list at most as many topics, partitions or offsets as a namespace may hold topics (50, set by MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE); a longer list is refused with 422. A request body may be 64 KiB; a larger one is refused with 413 before it is read.
  • A fetch asks each broker for at most 1 MiB of records. A broker still returns a first record larger than that, so a fetch can read a record of up to 8 MiB from each broker.
  • A reply holds at most 2 MiB of JSON. The records past that are left for the next fetch, which returns them first. A fetch always returns its first record, however large: a reply over 2 MiB holds that record alone and is sent in chunks, without a Content-Length.
  • A user may have 2 fetches in progress. A fetch past those is refused at once with 429 and error code 42901.
  • The service polls for 3 fetches at once, in turns of at most half a second, which fetches take in the order they ask. A turn that finds nothing goes to the back of the line; a turn that finds records keeps its place until its reply is sent. So a fetch whose records are ready waits about half a second for every 3 fetches ahead of it: about 1.5 s behind 11 quiet long polls, the most there can be, since the service holds 12 instances and an instance serves one fetch at a time. Replies being sent hold their turns longer. The default wait of 5000 ms gets through behind 11 quiet long polls; a shorter timeout can be refused. A fetch that gets no turn within its wait for records is refused with 429 and 42901. Like the refusal for a user's third fetch, it carries Retry-After: 1 and fetches nothing.
  • A reply must be sent within 30 s. A reply whose sending has begun and takes longer is not fetched again: the service closes the connection, and the next fetch starts after the reply's records. A reply over 2 MiB holds one record of up to 8 MiB, which takes up to about 10.7 MiB as base64 and up to 48 MiB as the JSON string of text of control characters, so a client may need to read such a reply at 1.6 MiB/s or faster. In binary, the reply for an 8 MiB record is about 10.7 MiB, which needs about 0.36 MiB/s. The skipped records stay in the topic, and the positions route can seek back to them, to the offset after the last record the client received, until a commit without a body, or auto-commit, commits past them. max_bytes does not make a one-record reply smaller.
  • A reply the client did not receive is fetched again by the next fetch, unless it was already handed to the network or took more than 30 s to send. This covers a client that leaves while its fetch polls or while a reply is sent, and a reply that fails to encode. The service cannot tell whether a client read a reply it handed to the network whole, so such a reply counts as received, as a reply read by a Kafka consumer does.
  • When a reply is cut at 2 MiB or at max_bytes, the partitions take turns to come first in the next replies, so one partition's records cannot keep another's out. Within a partition, records keep their order.

docs.text:
Every error reply of a consumer route is {"error_code": <int>, "message": <str>}, with two exceptions: a path that matches no route answers 404, and a method a route does not take answers 405, both with FastAPI's {"detail": <str>}. Error messages do not include Kafka's own error text.

docs.title: The earlier /api/v3 consumer routes
docs.text:
The consumer routes of earlier versions, under /api/v3/{namespace}/consumers, are removed, and a request to them is refused with 404, or with 405 for a group named recreate, whose path is the topic recreate route's. Clients use /api/v2/consumers, which acts in the caller's default namespace.

A client of the earlier routes also sees these changes:

  • A request body with a content type other than a v2 type or application/json is refused with 415. curl -d without -H "Content-Type: ..." sends application/x-www-form-urlencoded, so it is refused.
  • A create with a group or name that breaks the rule in Instances, fetches and commits is refused with 422, including an empty name, which the earlier routes took.
  • base_uri is an absolute URL. A client that built an instance's URL as the host followed by base_uri must use base_uri alone.
  • A fetch from a json instance must send Accept: application/vnd.kafka.json.v2+json. Without it, or with */*, it is refused with 406 and 40601, and with application/json with 406 and 406.
  • A json instance returns JSON keys and values as JSON values, not as strings, and records carry headers.
  • A json instance refuses a fetch whose first record has a key or value that is not UTF-8 with 408 and 40801, where the earlier routes returned it as base64. Read such records with a binary instance.
  • Replies have the content type application/vnd.kafka.v2+json, or a fetch's chosen v2 type, not application/json.
  • max_bytes counts bytes, a commit answers [], and GET …/offsets leaves out partitions never committed.

docs.title: Management API
docs.text:
The management routes create a user and its access key, list the user's namespaces and topics, and create, delete and recreate topics. They are under /api/v3:

Route Does POST /api/v3/user Creates the IAM user and the default namespace DELETE /api/v3/user Deletes the default namespace's topics, the namespace, the key and the IAM user POST /api/v3/key Returns the user's access key, creating the user, the namespace and the key if needed DELETE /api/v3/key Deletes the user's access keys GET /api/v3/namespace Lists the user's namespaces and their topics POST /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic} Creates a topic DELETE /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic} Deletes a topic and its records PUT /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic}/recreate Deletes a topic and creates it again, empty

Every route takes the subject and authorization headers (Getting subject and authorization) and no body. The examples use the variables that page exports: $SUBJECT, $AUTHORIZATION and $NAMESPACE.

The SDK's Client calls these routes with create_user, delete_user, create_key, delete_key, list_namespaces, create_topic, delete_topic and recreate_topic, in the default namespace. DiasporaDemo.ipynb shows them, and the Kafka producer and consumer that use the key.

docs.title: Replies
docs.text:
A management route answers HTTP 200 with a JSON object whose status says how the request went, so a client must read status, not the HTTP status:

  • "status": "success": the request was done. message says what was done, and each route adds its own fields, given below.
  • "status": "failure": the request was refused or failed. message says why; the messages are given below for each route.
  • "status": "error": the token check failed. reason says why, as in the table below, and nothing else is done.
{"status": "failure", "message": "Namespace ns-0123456789ab not found for 01234567-89ab-cdef-0123-456789abcdef"}

{"status": "error", "reason": "Token is inactive."}

The token check runs first on every route and fails with one of these reasons:

reason Cause Invalid user ID; expected UUID. subject is not a UUID Auth token must start with "Bearer ". authorization does not start with Bearer Invalid token format. The token after Bearer is not 33 to 254 letters, digits or underscores Token is inactive. Globus reports the token as expired, revoked or unknown Token does not belong to the user. The token's identity is not subject Not in the audience set. introspected = [...] server_client_id = ... The token is not for this service; the reason lists the token's audiences and the service's client ID Token lacks the scope for action. The token lacks the service's action_all scope

Two replies have a real HTTP status:

  • A request without the subject or authorization header answers 422 with FastAPI's {"detail": [...]}, which names each missing header.
  • An error the service does not handle, such as a DynamoDB or Globus Auth call that fails, answers 500 with the text Internal Server Error. What the request did before the error stays done; retry it, since every route can be repeated.

docs.title: Names and limits
docs.text:
• A user's default namespace is ns- followed by the last 12 characters of the subject without dashes, such as ns-0123456789ab for the subject 01234567-89ab-cdef-0123-456789abcdef. POST /api/v3/user and POST /api/v3/key create it. No route creates or deletes another namespace.
  • A topic name is 3 to 32 characters, each a letter, a digit, - or _, and does not start or end with - or _. Names are case-sensitive.
  • The topic my-topic of the namespace ns-0123456789ab is the Kafka topic ns-0123456789ab.my-topic. Every topic has one partition and replication factor 2.
  • A namespace holds at most 50 topics, a limit the service sets with the MAX_TOPICS_PER_NAMESPACE environment variable. Creating a new topic in a namespace that already holds that many returns "status": "failure" with a message that says to delete a topic first. Once a create adds a topic and leaves the namespace with at least 90% of the limit (45 of 50), the reply appends a warning to message and returns the same sentence in a warning field, which is absent otherwise. At 45 of 50 the warning reads "Namespace my-namespace now holds 45 of 50 topics; a create fails once it holds 50, so delete topics you no longer need." and at 50 of 50 it reads "Namespace my-namespace now holds 50 of 50 topics, the most allowed; delete a topic before you create another." Repeating the create of a topic that already exists, recreating a topic and deleting one are not limited.
  • The service tries each create or delete of a Kafka topic up to 3 times before it reports a failure.

Every route can be repeated: a second create of something that exists, or a delete of something that is gone, succeeds.

docs.title: Create user
docs.text:
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/user" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

POST /api/v3/user creates an IAM user named by the subject, and an IAM policy that lets it use, on the Kafka cluster, only topics, consumer group IDs and transactional IDs that start with the default namespace and a dot. It then creates the default namespace. A user, policy or namespace that already exists is kept. The route creates no access key: POST /api/v3/key does, and creates the user too, so a client that wants a key needs only that route.

{
  "status": "success",
  "message": "User 01234567-89ab-cdef-0123-456789abcdef created with namespace ns-0123456789ab",
  "subject": "01234567-89ab-cdef-0123-456789abcdef",
  "namespace": "ns-0123456789ab"
}
message of a failure Cause Failed to create IAM user: Failed to create user and policy: IAM did not complete the request IAM refused a call Failed to create namespace: Namespace already taken: <namespace> Another user holds the default namespace's name; the service deletes the IAM user

docs.title: Delete user
docs.text:
curl -X DELETE "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/user" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

DELETE /api/v3/user deletes, in this order: each topic of the default namespace, from the cluster and then from the namespace, with its records; the default namespace; the stored access key; and the IAM user, with its access keys and its policy. Consumer instances the user holds are not closed; they read nothing from the deleted topics. Deleting a user that does not exist succeeds.

{"status": "success", "message": "User 01234567-89ab-cdef-0123-456789abcdef deleted"}
message of a failure Cause Cannot delete user <subject>: user has <n> additional namespace(s). Delete namespaces first. The user holds namespaces other than the default one; nothing is deleted Failed to delete Kafka topic: Failed to delete Kafka topic <namespace>.<topic> after 3 attempts: the Kafka cluster did not complete it; retry shortly The cluster did not delete a topic. The topics deleted before it stay deleted; that topic, the rest, the namespace, the key and the user are kept Failed to delete IAM user: Failed to delete user and policy: IAM did not complete the request IAM refused a call. The topics, the namespace and the stored key are already deleted

docs.title: Create key
docs.text:
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/key" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

POST /api/v3/key returns the user's AWS access key and the cluster's endpoint:

  • If the service holds a key for the user, it returns that key, with "fresh": false and the message Access key already exists for <subject>. It creates nothing and does not check the key with IAM, so every call returns the same key until DELETE /api/v3/key deletes it.
  • Otherwise it creates the user and the default namespace as POST /api/v3/user does, deletes every access key the IAM user has, creates one, stores it, and returns it with "fresh": true.

To replace a key, delete it and create one.

{
  "status": "success",
  "message": "Access key created for 01234567-89ab-cdef-0123-456789abcdef",
  "access_key": "<access key ID>",
  "secret_key": "<secret access key>",
  "create_date": "2026-10-26T15:04:05+00:00",
  "endpoint": "<bootstrap servers>",
  "fresh": true
}

create_date is when IAM created the key, in ISO 8601 with a UTC offset. endpoint is the cluster's bootstrap servers for IAM authentication, a comma-separated list of host:port, or an empty string if the service has none set. The reply holds the secret key: keep it out of logs and notebooks you share.

The key lets a Kafka client connect to the cluster at endpoint, with MSK IAM authentication. Such a client may use only topics, consumer group IDs and transactional IDs that start with your default namespace and a dot, such as ns-0123456789ab.workers; the cluster refuses any other with an authorization error (GroupAuthorizationFailedError in kafka-python for a group).

message of a failure Cause Failed to create user: Failed to create IAM user: ... or Failed to create user: Failed to create namespace: ... Creating the user failed, as in Create user Failed to delete existing IAM access keys: Failed to delete access keys: IAM did not complete the request IAM refused to list or delete the user's keys Failed to create IAM access key: Failed to create access key: IAM did not complete the request IAM refused to create the key

If the service cannot store a new key, the reply is 500 and the key is not returned; a retry deletes it and creates another.

docs.title: Delete key
docs.text:
curl -X DELETE "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/key" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

DELETE /api/v3/key deletes every access key of the IAM user, then the key the service stores. Kafka clients can no longer connect with the key. The user, the namespace and the topics are kept, and the produce and consume routes, which take the Globus token, still work. Deleting a key that does not exist, or the key of a user that does not exist, succeeds.

{"status": "success", "message": "Access key deleted for 01234567-89ab-cdef-0123-456789abcdef"}
message of a failure Cause Failed to delete IAM access keys: Failed to delete access keys: IAM did not complete the request IAM refused to list or delete the keys. The stored key is kept, since it may still be valid

docs.title: List namespaces and topics
docs.text:
curl -X GET "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/namespace" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

GET /api/v3/namespace lists the user's namespaces and the topics each holds, both sorted by name. The topics are those the service records for the namespace, named without it; the route does not ask the cluster. A user not yet created has no namespaces.

{
  "status": "success",
  "message": "Found 1 namespaces for 01234567-89ab-cdef-0123-456789abcdef",
  "namespaces": {"ns-0123456789ab": ["my-topic", "other-topic"]}
}

The route fails only on the token check or with a 500.

docs.title: Topics
docs.text: The topic routes take the namespace and the topic, named without the namespace, in the path. The namespace must be one the user holds; for any other, a route fails with the message Namespace <namespace> not found for <subject>, and asks nothing of the cluster.

docs.title: Create topic
docs.text:
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/my-topic" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

POST /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic} checks the topic's name and the namespace, adds the topic to the namespace, and creates the Kafka topic. If the cluster does not create it, the route removes the topic from the namespace again. If the namespace already holds the topic, the reply is a success with the message Topic <topic> already exists in <namespace>, the topic is not counted again, and the Kafka topic is created if the cluster lacks it.

{"status": "success", "message": "Topic my-topic created in ns-0123456789ab", "topics": ["my-topic"]}

topics lists the namespace's topics after the create. Near the limit, message ends with a warning and the reply has a warning field (Names and limits).

message of a failure Cause Name must be between 3 and 32 characters The topic name is too short or too long Name can only contain letters, numbers, dash, and underscore The topic name has another character, such as a dot Name cannot start or end with hyphen or underscore The topic name starts or ends with - or _ Namespace <namespace> not found for <subject> The user does not hold the namespace Namespace <namespace> already holds 50 topics, the most allowed is 50; delete a topic to create another. The namespace is at the limit Namespace <namespace> holds <n> topics, more than the 50 allowed; delete <k> topic(s) to create another. The namespace is past the limit, which was lowered after it was filled Failed to create Kafka topic: Failed to create Kafka topic <namespace>.<topic> after 3 attempts: the Kafka cluster did not complete it; retry shortly The cluster did not create the topic

The name is checked before the namespace.

docs.title: Delete topic
docs.text:
curl -X DELETE "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/my-topic" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

DELETE /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic} deletes the Kafka topic, with every record in it, and then removes the topic from the namespace. A topic the cluster does not have counts as deleted. If the cluster does not delete the topic, the namespace keeps it, so a retry can delete it. A produce request to a deleted topic answers 404, and a consumer instance subscribed to it reads nothing from it.

{"status": "success", "message": "Topic my-topic deleted from ns-0123456789ab", "topics": ["other-topic"]}

topics lists the namespace's topics after the delete. Deleting a topic the namespace does not hold succeeds with the message Topic <topic> not found in <namespace>; the route still deletes the Kafka topic of that name if the cluster has one, and then says deleted.

message of a failure Cause Namespace <namespace> not found for <subject> The user does not hold the namespace Invalid topic name <topic> The topic name contains a dot. No other name rule is checked Failed to delete Kafka topic: Failed to delete Kafka topic <namespace>.<topic> after 3 attempts: the Kafka cluster did not complete it; retry shortly The cluster did not delete the topic

docs.title: Recreate topic
docs.text:
curl -X PUT "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/my-topic/recreate" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION"

PUT /api/v3/{namespace}/{topic}/recreate deletes the Kafka topic and creates it again with the same name, so the topic keeps its name and loses every record. The topic must be one the namespace holds, and the namespace's topics do not change. The route deletes the topic, waits 5 s, and creates it; while the cluster still holds the old topic, it tries the create again after 2 s, 3 times in all. So a recreate takes at least 5 s. Use it to empty a topic.

{"status": "success", "message": "Topic recreated"}
message of a failure Cause Namespace <namespace> not found for <subject> The user does not hold the namespace Topic <topic> not found in <namespace> The namespace does not hold the topic Failed to delete Kafka topic <namespace>.<topic> after 3 attempts: the Kafka cluster did not complete it; retry shortly The cluster did not delete the topic Failed to create Kafka topic <namespace>.<topic> after 3 attempts: it still exists; retry shortly The cluster was still deleting the old topic Failed to create Kafka topic <namespace>.<topic> after 3 attempts: the Kafka cluster did not complete it; retry shortly The cluster did not create the topic Kafka endpoint is not configured The service runs without a cluster

After a failed create the namespace still holds the topic, but the cluster may not: produce requests to it answer 404 until a retry of the recreate, or a create of the topic, makes it again.

docs.title: Produce API
docs.text:
The produce routes take the request syntax of Confluent's REST API v3, with the namespace in place of the cluster. They reply once every in-sync replica has acknowledged the record, so a client that only reaches port 443 can publish as well as consume.

Route Body Success POST /api/v3/{namespace}/topics/{topic}/records One record 200, the record's topic, partition, offset and timestamp POST /api/v3/{namespace}/topics/{topic}/records:batch {"entries": [...]}, 1 to 500 records 207, successes and failures

Both routes take the subject and authorization headers (Getting subject and authorization). The namespace in the path must be one the user holds, such as the default one, $NAMESPACE, and the topic one the namespace holds, named without the namespace; the management routes create topics.

The SDK's Client.produce and Client.produce_batch call these routes. ConsumerRESTDemo.ipynb produces records with plain HTTP requests and then with the SDK.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
# Produce one record
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/topics/my-topic/records" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"key": {"type": "STRING", "data": "job-42"},
       "value": {"type": "JSON", "data": {"step": 7, "loss": 0.31}},
       "headers": [{"name": "trace", "value": "AAE="}]}'

{"topic_name": "my-topic", "partition_id": 0, "offset": 12, "timestamp": "2026-10-26T15:04:05.123Z"}

# Produce a batch of records
curl -X POST "https://diaspora-web-service.qpp943wkvr7b2.us-east-1.cs.amazonlightsail.com/api/v3/$NAMESPACE/topics/my-topic/records:batch" \
  -H "subject: $SUBJECT" \
  -H "authorization: $AUTHORIZATION" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"entries": [
        {"id": "1", "value": {"type": "JSON", "data": {"step": 8}}},
        {"id": "2", "value": {"type": "AVRO", "data": {"step": 9}}}]}'

{
  "successes": [
    {"id": "1", "topic_name": "my-topic", "partition_id": 0, "offset": 13, "timestamp": "2026-10-26T15:04:05.456Z"}
  ],
  "failures": [
    {"id": "2", "error_code": 42206, "message": "value type AVRO needs a schema registry; Octopus runs no schema registry, so use BINARY, JSON or STRING"}
  ]
}

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
A produce request needs Content-Type: application/json; a charset parameter, if present, must be UTF-8. Any other content type is refused with 415.

A record has the optional fields key, value, headers, partition_id and timestamp, and needs a key or a value:

  • key and value are {"type": ..., "data": ...}. BINARY data is base64 and is written decoded; JSON data is any JSON value, written compactly as UTF-8; STRING data is a string, written as UTF-8. Absent or null data writes a null key or value. Octopus runs no schema registry, so the AVRO, PROTOBUF and JSONSCHEMA types, the schema fields (schema, schema_id, schema_version, subject, subject_name_strategy) and a key or value without a type are refused with 422.
  • A record whose key and value are both null or absent is refused with 400: kafka-python, which the service sends with, cannot send one.
  • headers is a list of {"name": string, "value": base64 string or null}; a null value is written as an empty one, because kafka-python cannot send a null header value.
  • partition_id may only be 0: every topic has one partition, and any other partition is not found (404).
  • timestamp is ISO-8601 with a UTC offset (for example 2026-10-26T15:04:05.123Z) and becomes the record's timestamp; without it, the record takes the time it is produced. The reply gives the record's timestamp in UTC.

docs.title: Batches
docs.text: The single-record route takes exactly one record: an empty body is refused with 422 and a body that holds more than one JSON value with 400. The batch route takes 1 to 500 entries, each a record with an id of 1 to 80 letters, digits, dashes or underscores that is distinct within the batch. It answers 207 once every entry has been acknowledged or has failed, within the 30 s, with each entry in successes or failures. An empty body, missing or empty entries, more than 500 entries, or a missing, invalid or repeated id refuses the whole batch with 422.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
A record holds at most 8 MiB (8,388,608 bytes), including about 100 bytes of Kafka's per-record overhead: its key, value and header names and values, once decoded, must fit in the rest. A request body holds at most 16 MiB, and so do a batch's records once encoded: JSON data is written compactly, but a number is written in full (1e15 as 1000000000000000.0), so a batch can grow past its body and is then refused with 413.

A body whose JSON would take too much memory to parse is refused with 413 before it is parsed. The service estimates the cost from the body's bytes and refuses an estimate over 192 MiB. The estimate counts 4 MiB for any body; w bytes for each byte of the body, where w is 1, 2 or 4 by the widest character the body holds or escapes (\u4e2d counts 2, \ud83d\ude00 counts 4); 2w + 2 bytes for each byte of JSON it may write, which can be longer than the body by up to 14 bytes for each number with an exponent and 3 for each decimal point; and 160 bytes for each { or [, 32 for each ", 40 for each , and 48 for each :. So a body of long ASCII strings or base64 passes up to the 16 MiB, a JSON array of four-digit numbers ([1000,1000,...]) up to about 14.5 MiB, a string of emoji up to about 13.4 MiB, an object with unique keys ({"1":1,"2":1,...}) up to about 9.9 MiB, an array of single digits or of numbers like 1e15 up to about 7.5 MiB, and one of empty objects or arrays ([{},{},...]) up to about 2.6 MiB.

The service holds at most 48 MiB of produce bodies and records at once, and at most 16 MiB for any one user (subject). A request holds the bytes of its body that have arrived, whatever its Content-Length declares, and once parsed the size of its records if that is larger. Once its body has arrived, a request takes one of the 8 places the service has for parsing and sending; a request still sending its body takes none. A user may have at most 2 requests in flight, at any stage. A request past a limit is refused with 429 and Retry-After: 1, as soon as it passes it: when it arrives, while its body arrives, or once it is read or parsed. When it arrives, a request is also refused before its body is sent if every place is taken or its Content-Length is more than the bytes free, for the service or for its user; nothing is held for it until its bytes arrive. A request's body must arrive within 20 s of its admission, which needs about 7 Mbit/s for a body of 16 MiB; a slower body is refused with 408. The service closes the connection after a 408, a 413 or a 429.

docs.title: Acknowledgement
docs.text:
The records' 30 s start once the body is read and parsed, and the records of a request share them to be acknowledged. A record not sent by then fails with 50003 and is not written; a record sent but not acknowledged by then fails with 50003 and may still be written. A 200 or a success in a 207 does not rule out a second copy either: the producer is not idempotent and retries a failed write within the 30 s, so a write that reached the cluster but whose acknowledgement was lost can be written twice. Consumers that need each record once should carry an id in the record and drop repeats.

Every topic has replication factor 2 on the cluster's two brokers, and the cluster's min.insync.replicas is 2, so a write needs both brokers to acknowledge it. While one broker restarts, for a cluster update or after a failure, the cluster refuses writes as NOT_ENOUGH_REPLICAS. The producer retries such a write until the record's 30 s are spent, and the record then fails with 50003 and the message "The cluster did not acknowledge the record in time; it may still be written": a single-record request answers 500, and a batch answers 207 with the entry in failures. Clients should retry such records with backoff, for example from 1 s doubling to 30 s, for at least as long as a broker takes to restart. Since the record may still be written, a retry can write it twice.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
While the service cannot reach the Kafka cluster, it answers 503 for 5 s before it tries again, with Retry-After set to the seconds left. A topic that the namespace holds but the cluster does not list answers 404 once the cluster has answered twice without it and 2 s have passed (a topic just created can take a moment to reach every broker). A failed token check answers 401 with {"status": "error", "reason": ...}, the body the management routes give for it, and a namespace or topic not found answers 404 with 40401. A request without the subject or authorization header answers 422 with FastAPI's {"detail": [...]}.

Code Status Meaning 40002 400 The topic name contains a dot 40003 400 The body is not one JSON object in UTF-8 40004 400 The body holds more than one JSON value 40005 400 A record field is invalid (bad base64, unknown type or field, timestamp without an offset, no key or value) 40301 403 The service is not authorized to write to the topic 40401 404 The namespace or topic is not found, in the namespace or in the cluster 40402 404 partition_id is not 0 40801 408 The body did not arrive within 20 s 41301 413 The request body is over 16 MiB 41302 413 A record is over 8 MiB, counting Kafka's overhead 41303 413 The body's JSON would take too much memory to parse 41304 413 A batch's records are over 16 MiB once encoded 41501 415 The body is not Content-Type: application/json in UTF-8 42206 422 The body is empty, or the record needs a schema registry 42208 422 The batch is empty or over 500 entries, or an entry's id is missing, invalid or repeated 42901 429 The service, or your share of it, holds as many produce requests or bytes as it can; retry after Retry-After 50002 500 Kafka refused the record, or the service is shutting down 50003 500 A retriable Kafka error, or the record was not acknowledged within the 30 s; retry it 50302 503 The service cannot reach the Kafka cluster; retry after Retry-After

In a batch, 40005, 40301, 40401 (from the cluster), 40402, 41302, 42206, 50002, 50003 and 50302 fail the one entry and the others go on; the other codes refuse the whole request. Error messages do not include Kafka's own error text.

docs.title: Differences from Confluent's REST API
docs.text:
The routes follow Confluent's statuses and codes except where noted here.

Case Octopus Confluent Why Body over 16 MiB 413, 41301 400, 400 413 says what is wrong, and the code tells it apart Record over 8 MiB 413, 41302 413, 413 A five-digit code like the rest Body not JSON, more than one value, invalid field 400 with 40003, 40004, 40005 400, 400 One code for each cause Content type not JSON 415, 41501 415, 415 A five-digit code like the rest More than one JSON value in a single-record body Refused Read as a stream of records One request is one record; several go to records:batch Schema fields with type BINARY, JSON or STRING Refused, 422 Ignored Without a schema registry the fields cannot mean what the client asked Payload errors in a record (a schema type or field, no type) 422, error_code 42206 422, error_code 422 and Error: 42206 : ... in the message The code where a client looks for it; Confluent already puts 42206 in error_code for an empty body and 42208 for an invalid batch, as here Token check failed 401 with status and reason 401 from the web server's HTTP authentication, without a Confluent error code; Confluent's 40101 is for a failed Kafka authentication The same body as the management routes partition_id above 0 404, 40402, at once Negative ids: 404, 40402. Ids past the partition count: the Kafka producer waits max.block.ms, then fails with "not present in metadata", which Confluent answers with 404, 40401 Every topic has one partition, so the answer is known at once No key and no value Refused, 400 Sent kafka-python cannot send it Null header value Written empty Written null kafka-python cannot send a null header value Too many requests or bytes 429, 42901 429, 429 for its own rate limit Confluent's code for a quota, which this is Topic missing from the cluster 404, 40401 after 2 s 404, 40401 after max.block.ms (60 s by default) Same reply, sooner Body slower than 20 s 408, 40801 No limit of its own; Confluent sends 408, 40801 for a serialization error A stalled upload would hold its share; the code is Confluent's for a 408 Parse cost, records over 16 MiB 413 with 41303, 41304 No such limits They bound the service's memory
